title: Alienation and the Young Marx
description: Species-being, the four kinds of alienation, and the critique of religion

concepts.title: From Hegel to Feuerbach to Marx
concepts.contentHtml:
The young Karl Marx (1818–1883) was trained as a Hegelian but soon broke with idealism. The hinge was Ludwig Feuerbach's Essence of Christianity (1841), which read theology as projection: the qualities humans attribute to God (love, wisdom, power) are alienated images of human capacities themselves.

Marx accepted the analysis but radicalised it. Feuerbach had located alienation in religious consciousness; Marx located it in material life. The reason humans need an imaginary God is that their actual existence — their labour, their social relations — has been emptied of meaning.

Famous formulation: religion is the 'sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world… the opium of the people.' Critique of religion is therefore the prelude to critique of the conditions that make religion necessary.

concepts.title: The Four Kinds of Alienation
concepts.contentHtml:
In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Marx distinguishes four senses in which the worker under capitalism is alienated:

From the product: what the worker makes belongs to the capitalist; the more she produces, the poorer she becomes relative to her output.
From the activity of labour: work becomes external, forced, a means to wages — not a self-expression.
From species-being: humans are characterised by free, conscious productive activity. Capitalist labour reduces this to a means of survival.
From other workers: cooperation in production becomes competition for jobs; fellow workers appear as rivals.

Alienation is not a feeling but a structure. The worker can be cheerful and still be alienated, because alienation describes the relation of the labourer to her labour and product, not her psychology.

concepts.title: Species-Being and Free Activity
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1844 Manuscripts develop a positive anthropology. What distinguishes humans from other animals is conscious productive activity: we transform nature according to plans we form in advance, and in transforming nature we transform ourselves. This capacity Marx calls species-being.

Capitalism turns this distinctive human activity into its opposite — drudgery imposed by external compulsion. Labour, which should be the medium of self-realisation, becomes the engine of self-loss.

The political horizon is therefore not redistribution alone but the abolition of conditions that estrange humans from their species capacity. Communism, in the early Marx's lyrical phrase, is 'the riddle of history solved' — a society where free, cooperative production replaces the alienated labour of class society.

title: Historical Materialism
description: Modes of production, base and superstructure, class struggle

concepts.title: Forces and Relations of Production
concepts.contentHtml:
The mature Marx (with Engels) advances historical materialism: a theory of how human societies change. Two paired terms do most of the work.

The forces of production are the material capacities a society can mobilise to produce: tools, technology, knowledge, labour power, raw materials. The relations of production are the social arrangements through which production is organised: who owns the means of production, who works for whom, how the product is distributed.

Different combinations define historical modes of production: ancient slave economies, feudal lord-and-serf, capitalism's wage labour. Each mode has its characteristic dynamics, contradictions, and patterns of class conflict.

concepts.title: Base and Superstructure
concepts.contentHtml:
From the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy: 'The mode of production of material life conditions the general process of social, political and intellectual life.'

The base is the economic structure — the totality of relations of production. The superstructure includes law, politics, religion, art, philosophy. The base does not mechanically determine the superstructure; rather it sets the framework within which superstructural forms develop and conditions which forms become dominant.

Later Marxists from Engels onward stressed that the relation is not one-way. Superstructural elements feed back: legal regimes stabilise property, ideology reproduces consent. The careful claim is one of conditioning and ultimate determination 'in the last instance', not of one-shot causation.

concepts.title: Class Struggle as the Motor of History
concepts.contentHtml:
The Communist Manifesto (1848) opens: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.'

A class is defined by its position in the relations of production — what it owns, what it must do to live. Capitalism's two principal classes are the bourgeoisie (owners of capital, who buy labour power) and the proletariat (those with nothing to sell but their labour).

History changes when the forces of production outgrow their relations. Feudal property fettered industrial capacity; capitalism shattered feudalism. In Marx's prediction the same dynamic would push capitalism beyond itself: socialised production under private appropriation generates crises and a class — the proletariat — both compelled and capable of overthrowing the system.

This prediction has not unfolded as Marx expected, but the analytical apparatus — class as a structural position, history as conflict over surplus — remains a powerful diagnostic tool.

title: Capital and the Critique of Political Economy
description: Commodities, labour theory of value, surplus value, fetishism

concepts.title: The Commodity and Its Two Faces
concepts.contentHtml:
Capital, Volume I (1867) opens with the commodity. A commodity has a use-value (it satisfies some human want — bread feeds, coats warm) and an exchange-value (it trades against other commodities at definite ratios — a coat for ten yards of linen).

What allows two qualitatively different things to exchange in fixed ratios? Marx argues it cannot be use-value (which is qualitative and incommensurable) nor demand alone. The common element is that both are products of abstract human labour measured in socially necessary labour time.

This is Marx's version of the labour theory of value he inherits from Smith and Ricardo and reworks. Value is not a property of objects in isolation but a social form that products of labour take when they are systematically produced for exchange.

concepts.title: Labour Power and Surplus Value
concepts.contentHtml:
Marx's central question: where does profit come from in a system of equal exchanges? Buying cheap and selling dear cannot explain profit at the level of the whole economy — what one capitalist gains another loses.

The answer turns on a special commodity: labour power. The capitalist buys not labour but the worker's capacity to labour, at its value (roughly the cost of subsistence and reproduction). But labour power, once set to work, can produce more value than it costs.

The working day divides into necessary labour (covering the wage) and surplus labour (producing surplus value appropriated by the capitalist). Profit is not theft in the moralistic sense; the exchange is 'fair' by capitalism's own rules. The exploitation is structural, embedded in the form of the wage relation itself.

concepts.title: Commodity Fetishism
concepts.contentHtml:
The famous Section 4 of Chapter 1 introduces commodity fetishism. In capitalist exchange, social relations between people take on the appearance of relations between things.

When I see a price tag, the fact that the commodity is worth a certain amount looks like a property of the object — as if the chair itself, by its nature, were 'worth' £100. In truth, that price expresses a definite social relation: the labour time of millions of producers, mediated by the market, congealing into the value of this object.

The 'fetish' is the misperception that confuses social relations for natural facts. Marx invokes the analogy of religious fetishism: just as worshippers attribute to wooden idols powers that are really their own, so capitalist subjects attribute to commodities and money powers that are really the powers of social labour. Critique reveals that what appears as the natural order of the market is a historically specific form of social life.

title: Hegemony and Ideology
description: Lenin, Gramsci, Althusser — why the ruling class rules

concepts.title: Lenin: Imperialism and the Vanguard
concepts.contentHtml:
V.I. Lenin (1870–1924) extended Marx in two influential directions. Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1916) argued that mature capitalism, with its monopolies and finance capital, exports capital abroad. Imperial expansion postpones internal crisis by securing markets and resources, while binding the world economy into a single hierarchical system.

What Is to Be Done? (1902) argued that workers, left to themselves, achieve only 'trade union consciousness' — fighting for higher wages within capitalism. Revolutionary consciousness must be brought from outside by a disciplined vanguard party of professional revolutionaries.

This thesis defined Bolshevik organisation and remains controversial. Critics inside and outside Marxism — Luxemburg, anarchists, council communists — saw in the vanguard the seed of post-revolutionary authoritarianism.

concepts.title: Gramsci: Hegemony and the Organic Intellectual
concepts.contentHtml:
Antonio Gramsci (1891–1937), imprisoned by Mussolini, asked why workers in advanced capitalist societies did not revolt despite repeated crises. His answer centred on hegemony.

Ruling classes do not rule by force alone but by securing consent through cultural, educational, religious, and media institutions — what Gramsci collectively called civil society. Their worldview becomes 'common sense', the unreflective horizon of the ruled.

Counter-hegemony therefore requires a long 'war of position' across cultural terrain, not just a 'war of manoeuvre' against the state. Central to this is the organic intellectual — thinkers rooted in their class, articulating its experience and forging its self-understanding, in contrast to the 'traditional intellectual' detached from material struggles.

concepts.title: Althusser: ISAs and Interpellation
concepts.contentHtml:
Louis Althusser (1918–1990) reread Marx through structuralism. In his 1970 essay 'Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses' he distinguished the repressive state apparatus (police, army, courts) from Ideological State Apparatuses (ISAs): schools, churches, family, media, unions. ISAs reproduce labour power and the relations of production by shaping subjects who 'spontaneously' accept their place.

His key concept is interpellation. Ideology 'hails' individuals as subjects: 'Hey, you there!' We turn around — and in turning, recognise ourselves as the one addressed. We become the kind of subject the system needs.

This account treats ideology not as false ideas in heads but as a material practice embedded in rituals, institutions, and routines. Even committed Marxists are interpellated — there is no clean exterior from which to know ideology without participating in it. The implication for politics is sobering: critique cannot rely on standing 'outside' the system it analyses.

title: Frankfurt School and Critical Theory
description: Adorno, Horkheimer, Marcuse, Habermas — culture industry and communicative action

concepts.title: The Dialectic of Enlightenment
concepts.contentHtml:
Theodor Adorno (1903–1969) and Max Horkheimer (1895–1973), founders of the Frankfurt School, wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947) in California exile. Their thesis is bleak: the Enlightenment project of mastering nature through reason has turned reason itself into instrumental reason — a mere calculation of efficient means, indifferent to ends.

The same rationality that defeats myth produces concentration camps and mass administration. Reason has not failed to be Enlightenment; Enlightenment, by its own logic, reverts to mythology in the form of bureaucratic domination.

This was not a rejection of reason but a demand that reason recover its self-critical capacity. Without that, the 'rational' organisation of life becomes a totally administered world.

concepts.title: The Culture Industry and Marcuse's Critique
concepts.contentHtml:
Adorno and Horkheimer coined culture industry to describe how mass-produced cultural goods (Hollywood films, pop music, radio) standardise consciousness while pretending to offer choice. The 'individuality' on offer is pseudo-individuation; even rebellion becomes a marketed style.

Herbert Marcuse (1898–1979) extended the analysis in One-Dimensional Man (1964). Late capitalism, he argued, neutralises opposition by absorbing it. Critical thought, art, even sexuality — all are flattened into the dimension of consumption. He called the result repressive desublimation: liberation that liberates nothing.

Marcuse became an icon of the 1960s student movement, which saw in his critique of advanced industrial society a rationale for radical cultural and political opposition.

concepts.title: Habermas and Communicative Action
concepts.contentHtml:
Jürgen Habermas (b. 1929), the leading second-generation Frankfurt theorist, agreed that instrumental reason is dangerous when generalised but refused the bleak conclusion. He distinguished instrumental rationality (oriented to success) from communicative rationality (oriented to mutual understanding).

In The Theory of Communicative Action (1981) he argues that everyday speech presupposes an 'ideal speech situation': claims to truth, rightness, and sincerity that participants must in principle be able to redeem with reasons. This counterfactual ideal grounds a discourse ethics: norms are valid when they could be agreed by all those affected under conditions of free, undistorted communication.

The diagnosis of late modernity then becomes the colonisation of the lifeworld: the spheres of communicative action (family, public sphere, civil society) are increasingly steered by money and power, distorting the conditions for authentic deliberation. The political project is to defend and expand the lifeworld against systemic encroachment.
